newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss turned back at least 30,000 refugees in WWII.
newsitem.headline: Swiss turned back at least 30,000 refugees in WWII.

text.p: Neutral Switzerland turned back at least 30,000 refugees seeking asylum during World War Two, triple the number previously acknowledged, researchers said on Wednesday.

The report by the Swiss Federal Archive and the Federal Bureau for Refugees cast new light on Switzerland's controversial wartime history and highlighted an era that many historians see as the country's darkest hour.

"Swiss authorities turned away more than 30,000 refugees -- 24,400 directly on the border and 14,500 asylum seekers who filed requests from abroad for permission to enter," the Swiss Federal Archive said in a statement.
The numbers do not add up because many people whose first petitions were rejected tried to cross into Switzerland anyway.

The study confirmed Switzerland took in 230,000 refugees, but its figures for those turned away go far beyond the figure of 10,000 cited in an official 1957 review of the country's wartime asylum practice.

Investigators examined 45,000 refugee dossiers from 1936 to 1946 in order to compile a record for more research and to answer a request from the Yad Vashem Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem for names of Jews who had been turned away.

They also reviewed the practices of border guards and delved into the records of border cantons for more insights because civil and military authorities destroyed most of the lists of rejected refugees after the war.

"Federal authorities' policy of deterrence was echoed at the cantonal level. Border units in direct contact with German authorities sought to prevent Jewish refugees from entering and...handed over refugees to French and German border police in France," it said in a summary of its findings.
"However, Switzerland took in around 230,000 refugees, including 22,000 Jews, on the basis of humanitarian considerations and international its obligations," it added.

Switzerland remained neutral but not untouched by the rise of the Nazis and their fascist allies in neighbouring Germany, Austria, Italy and France and the following waves of Jews seeking to escape genocide.
Swiss leaders in the 1930s, facing a far-right fringe at home that leaned toward the Nazis, opted to lock out Jews and other foreign refugees who they felt could spark instability.
In a major development, the government last year apologised for the first time for forcing Jewish refugees back to face near-certain death in their Nazi-controlled homelands.
It was a marked break from a still widespread view of Switzerland as a benign outsider to the bloody 1939-1945 war.
That view has also been tarnished by claims -- still being probed -- that Swiss banks still hold funds of Holocaust victims despite efforts by their heirs to find the dormant accounts.

In apologising for Switzerland's rejection of Jewish refugees in May 1995, then-President Kaspar Villiger said that the country had been frightened of neighbouring Germany as well as of the effect of mounting refugee numbers at home.
Pressure had mounted for an apology after the government finally acknowledged Berne had sought and achieved a secret 1938 deal with Adolf Hitler's Germany to keep out Jewish refugees.

Under the deal, Germany stamped passports held by Jews with a "J", allowing Swiss frontier guards to pick them out from other German travellers and turn them back. That deal extended to Austrian Jews after Germany absorbed its neighbour in 1938.
Switzerland only began allowing in some Jewish refugees again after the Allies landed in Normandy in 1944.
Only last year it posthumously rehabilitated a police chief convicted in 1940 of helping Jewish refugees.
